claim: MOSES is a systematic computational framework to quantify and discover cellular motion phenotypes.
source: Motion sensing superpixels (MOSES) is a systematic computational framework to quantify and discover cellular motion phenotypes
evidence: This is the title of the manuscript, which explicitly states the main purpose and nature of MOSES.

claim: Correct cell/cell interactions and motion dynamics are fundamental in tissue homeostasis.
source: Correct cell/cell interactions and motion dynamics are fundamental in tissue homeostasis, and defects in these cellular processes cause diseases.
evidence: This statement is presented as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Defects in cell/cell interactions and motion dynamics cause diseases.
source: Correct cell/cell interactions and motion dynamics are fundamental in tissue homeostasis, and defects in these cellular processes cause diseases.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact in the abstract.

claim: There is strong interest in identifying factors, including drug candidates that affect cell/cell interactions and motion dynamics.
source: Therefore, there is strong interest in identifying factors, including drug candidates that affect cell/cell interactions and motion dynamics.
evidence: This is presented as a logical consequence of the importance of cell interactions and motion dynamics.

claim: Existing quantitative tools for systematically interrogating complex motion phenotypes in timelapse datasets are limited.
source: However, existing quantitative tools for systematically interrogating complex motion phenotypes in timelapse datasets are limited.
evidence: This statement establishes the gap that MOSES aims to fill.

claim: MOSES measures and characterises biological motion with a unique superpixel 'mesh' formulation.
source: We present Motion Sensing Superpixels (MOSES), a computational framework that measures and characterises biological motion with a unique superpixel 'mesh' formulation.
evidence: This describes the key technical approach of MOSES.

claim: MOSES demonstrates single-cell tracking capability using published datasets.
source: Using published datasets, MOSES demonstrates single-cell tracking capability and more advanced population quantification than Particle Image Velocimetry approaches.
evidence: This claim is supported by testing on published datasets.

claim: MOSES provides more advanced population quantification than Particle Image Velocimetry approaches.
source: Using published datasets, MOSES demonstrates single-cell tracking capability and more advanced population quantification than Particle Image Velocimetry approaches.
evidence: This is a comparative claim supported by data analysis.

claim: MOSES analyzed more than 190 co-culture videos.
source: From > 190 co-culture videos, MOSES motion-mapped the interactions between human esophageal squamous epithelial and columnar cells mimicking the esophageal squamous-columnar junction, a site where Barrett's esophagus and esophageal adenocarcinoma often arise clinically.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the dataset size.

claim: Barrett's esophagus and esophageal adenocarcinoma often arise at the esophageal squamous-columnar junction.
source: From > 190 co-culture videos, MOSES motion-mapped the interactions between human esophageal squamous epithelial and columnar cells mimicking the esophageal squamous-columnar junction, a site where Barrett's esophagus and esophageal adenocarcinoma often arise clinically.
evidence: This is stated as clinical knowledge.

claim: MOSES is a powerful tool that will facilitate unbiased, systematic analysis of cellular dynamics from high-content time-lapse imaging screens.
source: MOSES is a powerful tool that will facilitate unbiased, systematic analysis of cellular dynamics from high-content time-lapse imaging screens with little prior knowledge and few assumptions.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the utility of MOSES.

claim: During tissue development and homeostasis in multicellular organisms, different cell types expand and migrate to form defined organ structures.
source: During tissue development and homeostasis in multicellular organisms, different cell types expand and migrate to form defined organ structures.
evidence: This is presented as established biological knowledge.

claim: During wound-healing, both immune and epithelial cells are required to proliferate and coordinately migrate.
source: For example, during wound-healing, both immune and epithelial cells are required to proliferate and coordinately migrate (Schaffer and Nanney, 1996; Clark, 2013; Leoni et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Aberrant cellular motion can be caused by deregulation of key signalling pathways in pathological conditions, including cancer.
source: Aberrant cellular motion can be caused by deregulation of key signalling pathways in pathological conditions, including cancer, and may be critical for disease development and progression, for example leading to invasion and metastasis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cancer biology.

claim: Aberrant cellular motion may be critical for disease development and progression, for example leading to invasion and metastasis.
source: Aberrant cellular motion can be caused by deregulation of key signalling pathways in pathological conditions, including cancer, and may be critical for disease development and progression, for example leading to invasion and metastasis.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the role of cellular motion in disease.

claim: When two cell populations adjoin in vivo, they often form a sharp, stable interface termed a 'boundary', with limited intermingling.
source: When two cell populations adjoin in vivo, they often form a sharp, stable interface termed a 'boundary', with limited intermingling (Dahmann et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: In adult humans, sharp boundaries separate different types of epithelia, such as between the squamous and columnar epithelia in the esophagus, cervix and anus.
source: In adult humans, sharp boundaries separate different types of epithelia, such as between the squamous and columnar epithelia in the esophagus, cervix and anus.
evidence: This is stated as anatomical knowledge.

claim: Disruption of these boundaries can lead to disease.
source: Disruption of these boundaries can lead to disease.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle.

claim: Disruption of the esophageal squamous columnar epithelial boundary is a feature of Barrett's Esophagus (BE).
source: For example, disruption of the esophageal squamous columnar epithelial boundary is a feature of Barrett's Esophagus (BE), a condition that confers a 30–50 fold increased risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) (Gaddam et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Barrett's Esophagus confers a 30–50 fold increased risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC).
source: For example, disruption of the esophageal squamous columnar epithelial boundary is a feature of Barrett's Esophagus (BE), a condition that confers a 30–50 fold increased risk of esophageal adenocarcinoma (EAC) (Gaddam et al., 2013).
evidence: This quantitative claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Live cell imaging over a long time (e.g. hours/days) is required to study the underlying complex cellular motion.
source: Live cell imaging over a long time (e.g. hours/days) is required to study the underlying complex cellular motion.
evidence: This is stated as a methodological requirement.

claim: There has been a rising interest in scaling up live cell imaging for unbiased high-throughput screening and analysis to identify drug targets and develop therapies that can cause or prevent abnormal cellular motion.
source: Recently, there has been a rising interest in scaling up live cell imaging for unbiased high-throughput screening and analysis to identify drug targets and develop therapies that can cause or prevent abnormal cellular motion (Schmitz et al., 2010; Held et al., 2010; Pau et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: A diverse range of co-culture experimental assays have been developed.
source: Accordingly, a diverse range of co-culture experimental assays have been developed (Goers et al., 2014), amongst which wound-healing type assays are one of the simplest and most widely used.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Wound-healing type assays are one of the simplest and most widely used co-culture experimental assays.
source: Accordingly, a diverse range of co-culture experimental assays have been developed (Goers et al., 2014), amongst which wound-healing type assays are one of the simplest and most widely used.
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of wound-healing assays.

claim: A major barrier is how to analyse the resulting complex biological motion phenotypes and its variation between different tested conditions, particularly for multi-cell type populations in high-content screens.
source: However, a major barrier is how to analyse the resulting complex biological motion phenotypes and its variation between different tested conditions, particularly for multi-cell type populations (Goers et al., 2014) in high-content screens.
evidence: This identifies a key challenge in the field.

claim: There are two types of cell movements: 'single-cell' migration in which each cell migrates independently or 'collective' migration where a group of cells migrates together in a coordinated fashion.
source: In general, there are two types of cell movements; 'single-cell' migration in which each cell migrates independently or 'collective' migration where a group of cells migrates together in a coordinated fashion.
evidence: This is stated as a classification of cell migration types.

claim: Single-cell migration has been well studied due to the availability of many single-cell tracking methods.
source: Single-cell migration has been well studied due to the availability of many single-cell tracking methods that can extract rich motion features even for unbiased high-throughput screens (Padfield et al., 2011; Meijering et al., 2012; Maška et al., 2014; Schiegg et al., 2015; Nketia et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Collective migration is much less understood due to a lack of tools to extract equally rich quantitative motion features of cell populations in a high-throughput fashion with minimal prior knowledge.
source: In contrast, collective migration is much less understood due to a lack of tools to extract equally rich quantitative motion features of cell populations in a high-throughput fashion with minimal prior knowledge.
evidence: This identifies a gap in the field that MOSES aims to address.

claim: Extension of existing single-cell tracking methods to analyse collective cell motion in general is non-trivial.
source: Extension of existing single-cell tracking methods to analyse collective cell motion in general is non-trivial.
evidence: This is stated as a technical challenge.

claim: Single-cell tracking methods all require accurate single-cell image segmentation, which is highly challenging when cells adjoin or overlap as they do frequently in tissue and confluent cell cultures.
source: Single-cell tracking methods all require accurate single-cell image segmentation, which is highly challenging when cells adjoin or overlap as they do frequently in tissue and confluent cell cultures.
evidence: This explains a limitation of single-cell tracking methods.

claim: There is a lack of systematic techniques to associate the motion of individual cells to the global moving collective.
source: Moreover, there is a lack of systematic techniques to associate the motion of individual cells to the global moving collective.
evidence: This identifies another gap in current methods.

claim: Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) and its variants do not require image segmentation.
source: Alternatively, existing popular methods to analyse collective motion in cell populations such as Particle Image Velocimetry (PIV) (Szabó et al., 2006; Petitjean et al., 2010) and its variants (e.g. cell image velocimetry (CIV) (Milde et al., 2012)), do not require image segmentation.
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of PIV methods, supported by citations.

claim: PIV methods only extract the global motion for a single video frame in the form of a velocity field, a velocity vector for each image pixel without assignment of pixels to individual cells.
source: However, they only extract the global motion for a single video frame in the form of a velocity field, a velocity vector for each image pixel without assignment of pixels to individual cells.
evidence: This describes a limitation of PIV methods.

claim: The lack of continuous tracking of cellular motion limits the application of PIV methods when characterising collective migration in complex biological phenomena such as boundary formation and chemoattraction.
source: This lack of continuous tracking of cellular motion limits the application of PIV methods when characterising collective migration in complex biological phenomena such as boundary formation and chemoattraction.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of PIV's limitations.

claim: PIV-extracted motion fields fail to exploit temporal continuity to reduce noise and avoid perturbations by imaging artefacts including visual clutter, image occlusion, and autofluorescence.
source: Furthermore, PIV-extracted motion fields fail to exploit temporal continuity to reduce noise and avoid perturbations by imaging artefacts including visual clutter, image occlusion, and autofluorescence.
evidence: This describes another limitation of PIV methods.

claim: PIV methods output only the velocities of image pixels.
source: Most prohibitively, PIV methods output only the velocities of image pixels.
evidence: This is stated as a key limitation of PIV.

claim: There is a lack of a systematic method to build motion 'signatures' to automatically and unbiasedly discriminate and predict biological motion phenotypes in large datasets.
source: There is a lack of a systematic method to build motion 'signatures' to automatically and unbiasedly discriminate and predict biological motion phenotypes in large datasets.
evidence: This identifies a gap that MOSES aims to fill.

claim: Previous studies have attempted to extract additional motion parameters from PIV and appearance parameters from individual video frames.
source: To this end, previous studies have attempted to extract additional motion parameters from PIV and appearance parameters from individual video frames (Neumann et al., 2006; Zaritsky et al., 2012; Zaritsky et al., 2014; Zaritsky et al., 2015; Zaritsky et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Previous approaches are sensitive to the number of identified phenotypes and data outliers, requiring relatively high-quality imaging.
source: However, these approaches are sensitive to the number of identified phenotypes and data outliers, requiring relatively high-quality imaging, restricting the experimental systems they can be applied to.
evidence: This describes limitations of previous approaches.

claim: All previous approaches assume prior knowledge of the motion behaviour.
source: Importantly, all the approaches (Neumann et al., 2006; Zaritsky et al., 2012; Zaritsky et al., 2014; Zaritsky et al., 2015; Zaritsky et al., 2017) assume prior knowledge of the motion behaviour.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous methods, supported by citations.

claim: Kymographs specifically exploit motion patterns known to be symmetrical around a given spatial axis such as wound healing and cannot be used to identify novel spatial motion features.
source: Notably, kymographs specifically exploit motion patterns known to be symmetrical around a given spatial axis such as wound healing and cannot be used to identify novel spatial motion features that could be relevant to normal tissue development or to a defined disease setting.
evidence: This describes a limitation of kymographs.

claim: A suitable computational method for studying cellular motion should be able to address the joint challenge of analysing single-cell and collective motion behaviour.
source: A suitable computational method for studying cellular motion therefore should be able to address the joint challenge of analysing single-cell and collective motion behaviour.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement for a suitable method.

claim: A suitable computational method must be scalable in a medium- or high-throughput manner.
source: Additionally, it must be: (i) scalable in a medium- or high-throughput manner
evidence: This is stated as a requirement.

claim: A suitable computational method must be sufficiently robust to handle inevitable variations in image acquisition and experimental protocol.
source: (ii) sufficiently robust to handle inevitable variations in image acquisition and experimental protocol
evidence: This is stated as a requirement.

claim: A suitable computational method must be sensitive to detect motion differences resulting from small changes in environment or stimuli with minimal replicates.
source: (iii) sensitive to detect motion differences resulting from small changes in environment or stimuli with minimal replicates
evidence: This is stated as a requirement.

claim: A suitable computational method must be automatic, requiring no manual intervention except for initial setting of parameters.
source: (iv) automatic, requiring no manual intervention except for initial setting of parameters
evidence: This is stated as a requirement.

claim: A suitable computational method must be unbiased to enable motion characterisation with minimal prior assumptions of motion behaviour.
source: (v) unbiased to enable motion characterisation (e.g. as a motion 'signature') with minimal prior assumptions of motion behaviour.
evidence: This is stated as a requirement.

claim: MOSES aims to provide a flexible and general approach for biological motion extraction, characterisation and phenotyping.
source: To address these analytical challenges, here we developed Motion Sensing Superpixels (MOSES), a computational framework that aims to provide a flexible and general approach for biological motion extraction, characterisation and phenotyping.
evidence: This states the aim of MOSES.

claim: MOSES empowered PIV-type methods with a mesh formulation that enables systematic measurement and unbiased extraction of rich motion features for single and collective cell motion suitable for high-throughput phenotypic screens.
source: We empowered PIV-type methods with a mesh formulation that enables systematic measurement and unbiased extraction of rich motion features for single and collective cell motion suitable for high-throughput phenotypic screens.
evidence: This describes how MOSES improves upon PIV methods.

claim: MOSES can be used to effectively 'encode' complex dynamic patterns in the form of a motion 'signature'.
source: Our analysis illustrates how MOSES can be used to effectively 'encode' complex dynamic patterns in the form of a motion 'signature', which would not be possible using standard globally extracted velocity-based measures from PIV.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of MOSES demonstrated in the analysis.

claim: MOSES can highlight novel motion phenotypes in high-content comparative biological video analysis.
source: In particular, MOSES can highlight novel motion phenotypes in high-content comparative biological video analysis.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of MOSES.

claim: Three epithelial cell lines were used in pairwise combinations in the experimental model system.
source: To recapitulate features of the in vivo boundary formation, we used three epithelial cell lines in pairwise combinations and an experimental model system with similar characteristics to wound-healing and migration assays but with additional complexity.
evidence: This describes the experimental setup.

claim: EPC2 is an immortalised squamous epithelial cell line from the normal esophagus.
source: EPC2, an immortalised squamous epithelial cell line from the normal esophagus (Harada et al., 2003)
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the cell line, supported by a citation.

claim: CP-A is an immortalised BE cell line with gastric columnar epithelial properties.
source: CP-A, an immortalised BE cell line with gastric columnar epithelial properties (Merlo et al., 2011)
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the cell line, supported by a citation.

claim: OE33 is derived from EAC.
source: OE33, derived from EAC (Boonstra et al., 2010)
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the cell line, supported by a citation.

claim: Green and red fluorescent-labelled EPC2, CP-A, and OE33 cells proliferated at the same rate.
source: Green and red fluorescent-labelled EPC2, CP-A, and OE33 cells proliferated at the same rate (Figure 1D, for EPC2 cells: slope = 0.976, Pearson correlation coefficient 0.978, Figure 1—figure supplement 1E)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in figures.

claim: Green and red fluorescent-labelled EPC2, CP-A, and OE33 cells migrated in a similar way.
source: and migrated in a similar way (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: Compared to non-dyed cells, the mobility of CP-A cells were unaffected by dyes.
source: Compared to non-dyed cells, the mobility of CP-A cells were unaffected however both dyes equally reduced the mobility of EPC2 and OE33 cells.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: Both dyes equally reduced the mobility of EPC2 and OE33 cells compared to non-dyed cells.
source: Compared to non-dyed cells, the mobility of CP-A cells were unaffected however both dyes equally reduced the mobility of EPC2 and OE33 cells.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: The diffusion modes of all cells were unaffected by dyes.
source: The diffusion modes of all cells were unaffected (Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: The boundary formation behaviour between dyed and non-dyed cells was identical.
source: and the boundary formation behaviour between dyed and non-dyed cells was identical.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: In the EPC2:EPC2 combination, the green- or red-labelled cells met and coalesced into a monolayer.
source: Firstly, in the squamous combination using the same EPC2 cell line labelled with two different colours, the green- or red-labelled EPC2:EPC2 cells met and coalesced into a monolayer as expected.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: In the EPC2:CP-A combination, boundary formation was observed between the two populations after 72 h, following a short period of CP-A 'pushing' EPC2.
source: Secondly, in the squamous-columnar EPC2:CP-A combination, we observed boundary formation between the two populations after 72 h, following a short period of CP-A 'pushing' EPC2.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: In the EPC2:OE33 combination, the cancer cell line OE33 expanded continuously, resulting in the disappearance of EPC2 from the field of view.
source: Thirdly, in the squamous-cancer EPC2:OE33 combination, the cancer cell line OE33 expanded continuously, resulting in the disappearance of EPC2 from the field of view (Video 2, Figure 1E)
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments, supported by video and figure.

claim: The observed phenotypes were not due to differential proliferation rate between the individual cell lines in combination.
source: Interestingly, cell counting suggests the observed phenotypes were not due to differential proliferation rate between the individual cell lines in combination (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by cell counting data shown in a figure.

claim: Culturing of the same cell combinations in serum-free versus 5% serum medium had undetectable impact on cell density at the very confluent cell conditions investigated.
source: We observed that culturing of the same cell combinations in serum-free versus 5% serum medium had undetectable impact on cell density at the very confluent cell conditions investigated (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: Serum-free condition induced large global changes in cell migration.
source: However, as expected, serum-free condition induced large global changes in cell migration (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 5A)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in figures.

claim: Serum-free condition resulted in observed loss of cell contacts and collective sheet migration.
source: with observed loss of cell contacts, collective sheet migration (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B,C)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: Serum-free condition resulted in the absence of boundary formation.
source: and the absence of boundary formation.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments.

claim: Serum-free condition resulted in reduced overall boundary displacement.
source: We also observed reduced overall boundary displacement (Figure 1F,G)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in figures.

claim: In serum-free medium, all cell line combinations exhibited similar motion dynamics.
source: and all cell line combinations exhibited similar motion dynamics (Figure 1F,G, Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in figures and video.

claim: MOSES was formulated modularly with three components: motion extraction, construction of long-time motion tracks, and capture of local dynamic context.
source: MOSES was formulated modularly with three components (Figure 2): 1) motion extraction; 2) construction of long-time motion tracks; and 3) capture of local dynamic context.
evidence: This describes the structure of MOSES, illustrated in a figure.

claim: MOSES uses dense optical flow to avoid the shortcomings of using cell segmentation to track individual cells in confluent tissue.
source: We use dense optical flow to avoid the shortcomings of using cell segmentation to track individual cells in confluent tissue.
evidence: This describes a design choice in MOSES.

claim: Optical flow is similar to particle image velocimetry (PIV) but yields higher resolution motion fields with a displacement vector for each pixel at every time point.
source: Optical flow is similar to particle image velocimetry (PIV) but yields higher resolution motion fields with a displacement vector for each pixel at every time point.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between optical flow and PIV.

claim: PIV typically estimates a single velocity for an image patch or 'window' using spatial correlation.
source: PIV typically estimates a single velocity for an image patch or 'window' using spatial correlation.
evidence: This describes how PIV works.

claim: Optical flow is easier to modify to account for additional physical phenomena such as out-of-plane motion and large, discontinuous movements not captured within a PIV 'window'.
source: Optical flow is also easier to modify to account for additional physical phenomena such as out-of-plane motion and large, discontinuous movements not captured within a PIV 'window' (Brox et al., 2004; Brox et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: MOSES constructs long-time motion tracks that continuously track the cellular motion for any amount of time using superpixels.
source: To capture all spatial motion dynamics in the video, we construct long-time motion tracks that continuously track the cellular motion for any amount of time using superpixels.
evidence: This describes a key feature of MOSES.

claim: MOSES validated its motion extraction and long-time track construction using published single-cell tracking datasets from the cell tracking challenge.
source: We validated our motion extraction and long-time track construction using published single-cell tracking datasets from the cell tracking challenge (Maška et al., 2014) (Video 3)
evidence: This describes validation of MOSES, supported by citation and video.

claim: MOSES produced very similar tracks (similarity score of 0.8) to TrackMate in spike-in experiments.
source: Our method produced very similar tracks (similarity score of 0.8) to an open software tool for single-particle tracking, TrackMate (Tinevez et al., 2017) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, Video 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative comparison and figures/video.

claim: A 'mesh' is constructed by 'linking' superpixels to capture how individual superpixels move with respect to their neighbours over time.
source: A 'mesh' is constructed by 'linking' superpixels to capture how individual superpixels move with respect to their neighbours over time (Figure 2A, Step 6).
evidence: This describes a key component of MOSES, illustrated in a figure.

claim: The constructed dynamic mesh naturally captures the local collective dynamics without explicit thresholding or clustering.
source: The constructed dynamic mesh, inspired by work in human surveillance (Chang et al., 2011), naturally captures the local collective dynamics without explicit thresholding or clustering.
evidence: This describes a property of the mesh, with citation to related work.

claim: The mesh can be used to derive robust local and global measures of motion relating to biological phenomena such as collective motion and tissue interactions.
source: Because the mesh is a representation of interactions inferred from the local spatial relationships of superpixels, it can be used to derive robust local and global measures of motion relating to biological phenomena such as collective motion and tissue interactions (see below).
evidence: This describes the utility of the mesh.

claim: In total, 125 videos (48 with 0% serum and 77 with 5% serum) were collected from four independent experiments and jointly analysed.
source: In total, 125 videos (48 with 0% serum and 77 with 5% serum) were collected from four independent experiments and jointly analysed.
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the dataset.

claim: Standard velocity kymographs confirmed observations of differences in cell motion between 0% and 5% serum conditions.
source: Standard velocity kymographs were able to firstly confirm our observations in Figure 1E–G of the differences in cell motion between 0% and 5% serum conditions.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the analysis.

claim: All cell combinations grown in 0% serum exhibited a similar global motion pattern, minimal sheet-like motion and interface movement following gap closure.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, all cell combinations grown in 0% serum exhibited a similar global motion pattern, minimal sheet-like motion and interface movement following gap closure.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: In 5% serum the three cell line combinations exhibited very different dynamics.
source: By contrast, in 5% serum the same three cell line combinations exhibited very different dynamics
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the analysis.

claim: Formation of a stable equilibrium following contact was observed only between EPC2 and CP-A cell sheets in 5% serum.
source: amongst which we observed the formation of a stable equilibrium following contact only between EPC2 and CP-A cell sheets.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the analysis.

claim: Speed was an insufficient metric to characterise the observed phenotypes, exhibiting high variance between replicates and failure to highlight the uniqueness of the EPC2:CP-A interaction.
source: As shown in Figure 3B, aside from an indication of a global speed increase in 5% serum, speed was an insufficient metric to characterise the observed phenotypes, exhibiting high variance between replicates and failure to highlight the uniqueness of the EPC2:CP-A interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: MOSES designed four different additional measures to quantitatively distinguish between different combinations of the three cell lines: boundary formation index, mesh stability index, mesh order, and maximum velocity cross-correlation.
source: Using MOSES, we constructed a motion saliency map for visualising global motion patterns (Figure 3—figure supplement 2) and designed four different additional measures as summarised in Table 1 to quantitatively distinguish between different combinations of the three cell lines (EPC2, CP-A and OE33) used in our assay: i) boundary formation index, based on the degree that motion concentrates into a local spatial region (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3); ii) mesh stability index, which measures the degree of movement between neighbouring cell groups locally within the sheet at the endpoint (Figure 3—figure supplement 4); iii) mesh order to measure the degree of collective motion of the whole sheet (Figure 3—figure supplement 5, Video 5) and iv) the maximum velocity cross-correlation, which measures the average correlation in motion between the two epithelial sheets from their movement history (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This describes the measures developed using MOSES, supported by figures and table.

claim: The boundary formation index was highest (median 0.74) for EPC2:CP-A grown in 5% serum (n = 30/77).
source: The boundary formation index was highest (median 0.74) for EPC2:CP-A grown in 5% serum (n = 30/77) (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 8B)
evidence: This is a quantitative result supported by figures.

claim: EPC2:EPC2 and EPC2:OE33 in 5% serum were below the boundary formation cut-off.
source: whilst EPC2:EPC2 and EPC2:OE33 in 5% serum were below the boundary formation cut-off.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the analysis.

claim: In 5% serum, EPC2:CP-A had the highest mesh stability index (median 0.90), compared to EPC2:EPC2 (0.76) and EPC2:OE33 (0.25).
source: In 5% serum, EPC2:CP-A had the highest mesh stability index (median 0.90), compared to EPC2:EPC2 (0.76) and EPC2:OE33 (0.25) (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 8C).
evidence: This is a quantitative result supported by figures.

claim: Only the squamous-columnar combination (EPC2:CP-A) formed a final stable boundary.
source: Together these results illustrate that only the squamous-columnar combination (EPC2:CP-A) formed a final stable boundary.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the results.

claim: In 0% serum, no difference in velocity cross-correlation across all combinations was found before and after gap closure.
source: In 0% serum, no difference in velocity cross-correlation across all combinations was found before and after gap closure (Figure 3E )
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: CP-A:OE33 (Barrett's:cancer, n = 6) exhibited a substantial increase in VCC following gap closure (0.03 to 0.17).
source: Interestingly, CP-A:OE33 (Barrett's:cancer, n = 6) also exhibited a substantial increase in VCC following gap closure (0.03 to 0.17) (Figure 3—figure supplement 8D,E)
evidence: This is a quantitative result supported by a figure.

claim: No substantial increase in VCC was observed for CP-A:CP-A (0.01 to 0.06).
source: but no substantial increase was observed for CP-A:CP-A (0.01 to 0.06) (Figure 3—figure supplement 8D,E)
evidence: This is a quantitative result supported by a figure.

claim: Both the velocity order parameter and mesh order parameter indicate clear overall reduction in collective motion in cells grown in 0% serum compared to 5% serum.
source: Both the velocity order parameter and our mesh order parameter (Figure 3F,G) indicate clear overall reduction in collective motion in cells grown in 0% serum compared to 5% serum.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in figures.

claim: Clear infiltration with 'finger-like' protrusions of CP-A into the OE33 cell sheet was observed in CP-A:OE33 grown in 5% serum.
source: Interestingly, we found non-invading boundaries in all cell line combinations except CP-A:OE33, where we observed clear infiltration with 'finger-like' protrusions of CP-A into the OE33 cell sheet grown in 5% serum (Figure 3—figure supplement 10B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: No 'finger-like' protrusions or significant intermixing of cells were detected in EPC2:CP-A under 5% serum conditions.
source: No such 'finger-like' protrusions or significant intermixing of cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 10D,F–H) were detected in EPC2:CP-A under the same conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in figures.

claim: Among all tested cell-type combinations, an 'interacting' final stable boundary was detected uniquely in the squamous-columnar EPC2:CP-A combination grown in 5% serum.
source: Altogether, our characterisation suggests that, among all tested cell-type combinations, we detect an 'interacting' final stable boundary uniquely in the squamous-columnar EPC2:CP-A combination grown in 5% serum (Video 6).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the characterization, supported by video.

claim: The epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is frequently mutated in EAC.
source: The epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is frequently mutated in EAC, sometimes overexpressed in BE and is activated by bile acid reflux, the main observed cause of BE clinically (Dixon et al., 2001; Souza, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: EGFR is sometimes overexpressed in BE.
source: The epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is frequently mutated in EAC, sometimes overexpressed in BE and is activated by bile acid reflux, the main observed cause of BE clinically (Dixon et al., 2001; Souza, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: EGFR is activated by bile acid reflux, the main observed cause of BE clinically.
source: The epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) is frequently mutated in EAC, sometimes overexpressed in BE and is activated by bile acid reflux, the main observed cause of BE clinically (Dixon et al., 2001; Souza, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: A total of 40 videos (each 144 h, one frame per h) were collected from three independent experiments for the EGF addition study.
source: A total of 40 videos (each 144 h, one frame per h) were collected from three independent experiments, in a 24-well plate medium-throughput screen (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about the dataset.

claim: With increasing EGF, the boundary position was displaced a distance farther from the initial point of contact between the two cell populations.
source: With increasing EGF, the boundary position was displaced a distance farther from the initial point of contact between the two cell populations, with slightly enhanced cell speed and decreased boundary coherence (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in figures.

claim: With increasing EGF, cell speed was slightly enhanced.
source: With increasing EGF, the boundary position was displaced a distance farther from the initial point of contact between the two cell populations, with slightly enhanced cell speed and decreased boundary coherence (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in figures.

claim: With increasing EGF, boundary coherence decreased.
source: With increasing EGF, the boundary position was displaced a distance farther from the initial point of contact between the two cell populations, with slightly enhanced cell speed and decreased boundary coherence (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in figures.

claim: At 0 ng/ml EGF, the normalised strain curve linearly increases before plateauing around 72 h.
source: at 0 ng/ml EGF, the curve linearly increases before plateauing around 72 h
evidence: This describes the shape of the curve at 0 ng/ml EGF.

claim: As EGF concentration increases, the normalised strain curve becomes more linear and the plateau is lost above 5 ng/ml.
source: as EGF concentration increases, the curve becomes more linear and the plateau is lost above 5 ng/ml.
evidence: This describes how the curve changes with EGF concentration.

claim: The boundary formation index decreased with increasing EGF (0.74 at 0 ng/ml to 0.46 at 20 ng/ml, comparable to EPC2:OE33 without EGF (0.46)).
source: The boundary formation index decreased with increasing EGF (0.74 at 0 ng/ml to 0.46 at 20 ng/ml, comparable to EPC2:OE33 without EGF (0.46)), indicating loss of the boundary (i.e. index below the 0.69 cut-off) (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result supported by a figure.

claim: The mesh stability index decreased from 0.94 (stable, 0 ng/ml EGF) to 0.72 (unstable, 20 ng/ml).
source: The mesh stability index decreased from 0.94 (stable, 0 ng/ml EGF) to 0.72 (unstable, 20 ng/ml) (Figure 4G)
evidence: This is a quantitative result supported by a figure.

claim: The maximum VCC difference before and after gap closure decreased from 0.16 (0 ng/ml EGF) to 0.04 (20 ng/ml EGF).
source: since the maximum VCC difference before and after gap closure decreased from 0.16 (0 ng/ml EGF) to 0.04 (20 ng/ml EGF) (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a quantitative result supported by a figure.

claim: Above 5 ng/ml EGF, the phenotype of EPC2:CP-A becomes similar to that between EPC2 and the EAC cell line, OE33.
source: Together these measures show that above 5 ng/ml EGF, the phenotype of EPC2:CP-A becomes similar to that between EPC2 and the EAC cell line, OE33 (Video 7).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the measures, supported by video.

claim: Cell counting and quantification of fluorescence decay suggest cell division is not the primary factor influencing the boundary at the cell density used in experiments in 5% serum.
source: Cell counting and quantification of fluorescence decay suggest cell division is not the primary factor influencing the boundary at the cell density used in our experiments in 5% serum (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: Titrating EGF did not rescue the effect of serum absence, with non-significant changes in the boundary formation index (0 ng/ml: 0.60 ± 0.07, 20 ng/ml: 0.65 ± 0.03) and maximum velocity cross-correlation.
source: Of note, titrating EGF did not rescue the effect of serum absence, with non-significant changes in the boundary formation index (0 ng/ml: 0.60 ± 0.07, 20 ng/ml: 0.65 ± 0.03) and maximum velocity cross-correlation, although the mesh stability index decreased, likely due to increased cell movement (Figure 4—figure supplement 2 (n = 25)).
evidence: This is a quantitative result supported by a figure.

claim: Using both the velocity order parameter and mesh order index, little change in collective motion was found upon EGF addition in 0% serum.
source: Using both the velocity order parameter and mesh order index to characterise collective motion, we found little change in collective motion upon EGF addition in 0% serum (Figure 4—figure supplement 2J,K)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: In 5% serum plus EGF, raising EGF concentration increased velocity order but decreased mesh order.
source: However, in 5% serum plus EGF, the two measures exhibited opposite results: raising EGF concentration increased velocity order but decreased mesh order, Figure 4I,J.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in figures.

claim: The mesh order, by explicitly accounting for the motion of neighbouring cells, better reflects human observation of motion in videos than velocity order.
source: We note however that the mesh order, by explicitly accounting for the motion of neighbouring cells, better reflects human observation of motion in videos (Videos 5–7).
evidence: This is stated as an observation, supported by videos.

claim: Cell counting for 0% serum suggested minimal influence of cell proliferation.
source: Cell counting for 0% serum again suggested minimal influence of cell proliferation (Figure 4—figure supplement 2L,M).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: Principal component analysis (PCA) was applied to the normalised mesh strain curves of the 77 videos of all cell line combinations cultured in 5% serum conditions to learn the principal component vectors that define the x-y axis of the 2D map.
source: To position each video on a 2D map, we applied principal component analysis (PCA) to the normalised mesh strain curves of the 77 videos of all cell line combinations cultured in 5% serum conditions to learn the principal component vectors that define the x-y axis of the 2D map.
evidence: This describes the method used to generate the motion map.

claim: The constructed PCA map of the 77 videos from cells cultured in 5% serum shows that this unbiased approach automatically clusters all videos corresponding to each cell line combination.
source: The constructed PCA map of the 77 videos from cells cultured in 5% serum (Figure 5B) shows that this unbiased approach automatically clusters all videos corresponding to each cell line combination.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: The videos were ordered in a continuous manner, as shown by the increasingly linear shape of the mean normalised strain curve when looking left to right across the plot from CP-A:CP-A to EPC2:OE33.
source: Furthermore, the videos were ordered in a continuous manner, as shown by the increasingly linear shape of the mean normalised strain curve when looking left to right across the plot in Figure 5B from CP-A:CP-A to EPC2:OE33.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: This clustering was not achieved with root mean squared displacement (RMSD), the non-mesh version of the MOSES-normalised mesh strain curve.
source: This clustering was not achieved with root mean squared displacement (RMSD), the non-mesh version of the MOSES-normalised mesh strain curve (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison shown in a figure.

claim: The clustering appears independent of the particular dimensionality reduction technique used.
source: Moreover, it appears independent of the particular dimensionality reduction technique used (Figure 5—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: The 1D MOSES-based motion signatures trained a machine learning classifier with no further processing to predict cell combination identity better than RMSD.
source: Finally, the 1D MOSES-based motion signatures trained a machine learning classifier with no further processing to predict cell combination identity better than RMSD (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: The videos from 0% serum mapped to a different area of the 2D plot than 5% serum videos, whilst preserving the continuous ordering of the previous videos.
source: The videos from 0% serum mapped to a different area of the 2D plot, whilst preserving the continuous ordering of the previous videos.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the motion map.

claim: Without having watched the videos, it is easy to predict that the cells have markedly different motion dynamics in 0% serum compared to 5% serum based on the motion map.
source: Therefore, without having watched the videos, it is easy to predict that the cells have markedly different motion dynamics in 0% serum compared to 5% serum.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the motion map.

claim: Since the points for the 5% serum videos cover a larger area of the 2D plot than the 0% serum videos, one can predict more diversity of motion in 5% serum.
source: Furthermore, since the points for the 5% serum videos cover a larger area of the 2D plot than the 0% serum videos, one can predict more diversity of motion in 5% serum (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the motion map, supported by a figure.

claim: With increasing EGF, the squamous-columnar EPC2:CP-A motion dynamics become increasingly similar to squamous-cancer EPC2:OE33 above 5 ng/ml.
source: With increasing EGF, the squamous-columnar EPC2:CP-A motion dynamics become increasingly similar to squamous-cancer EPC2:OE33 above 5 ng/ml, as evidenced by the square points moving from the area of blue circular EPC2:CP-A points into the area of orange circular EPC2:OE33 points.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the motion map.

claim: The motion map is consistent with the result using the specific derived measures.
source: Thus our motion map is consistent with the result using the specific derived measures (above).
evidence: This is stated as a validation of the motion map approach.

claim: Motion fields inferred from optical flow by MOSES were similar to those from PIV, yielding both similar speed curves and velocity kymographs.
source: Reanalysing the datasets with MOSES, we found that motion fields inferred from optical flow by MOSES were similar to those from PIV, yielding both similar speed curves and velocity kymographs.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the comparison.

claim: MOSES exhibited greater sensitivity to salient motion events than PIV.
source: However, MOSES exhibited greater sensitivity to salient motion events (indicated in Figure 6A).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison shown in a figure.

claim: MOSES superpixel tracks are a more data-efficient encoding of the spatio-temporal velocity distribution than PIV velocity vectors.
source: Compared to PIV velocity vectors, MOSES superpixel tracks are a more data-efficient (see Discussion) encoding of the spatio-temporal velocity distribution that naturally enhances and preserves the salient motion.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between MOSES and PIV.

claim: Reconstructed velocity kymographs from the MOSES motion trajectories capture not only the pattern of the full velocity kymograph but further selectively enhanced the detection of the deformation wave signature formed at the interface between EphB2/ephrinB1 epithelial monolayers.
source: Reconstructed velocity kymographs from the MOSES motion trajectories capture not only the pattern of the full velocity kymograph but further selectively enhanced the detection of the deformation wave signature formed at the interface between EphB2/ephrinB1 epithelial monolayers (as indicated in Figure 6A, right panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: All velocity-based statistics that can be derived from PIV are fully preserved in MOSES.
source: Thus, all velocity-based statistics that can be derived from PIV, such as the velocity order parameter, are fully preserved in MOSES.
evidence: This is stated as a property of MOSES.

claim: Instantaneous velocity-based measures from single videos commonly derived from PIV are noisy.
source: Firstly, instantaneous velocity-based measures from single videos commonly derived from PIV are noisy.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of PIV.

claim: The velocity order parameter variation for the slower MCF-10A control cells is non-smooth and highly variable between consecutive time points.
source: For example, the velocity order parameter variation for the slower MCF-10A control cells is non-smooth and highly variable between consecutive time points (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: The MOSES mesh order exploits long-time continuity and neighbourhood relations to robustly capture collective motion in a manner consistent with human observation.
source: In contrast, the MOSES mesh order exploits long-time continuity and neighbourhood relations to robustly capture collective motion in a manner consistent with human observation (Video 5).
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of MOSES, supported by video.

claim: Long-time MOSES tracks and superpixel mesh strain curves can unbiasedly cluster the global motion pattern into small spatio-temporal groups.
source: Secondly, long-time MOSES tracks and superpixel mesh strain curves can unbiasedly cluster the global motion pattern into small spatio-temporal groups (Figure 6C, Video 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure and video.

claim: The computation of motion saliency maps from forward and backward tracked frames effectively highlight the spatial concentration of motion.
source: The computation of motion saliency maps from forward and backward tracked frames effectively highlight the spatial concentration of motion
evidence: This is stated as a capability of MOSES.

claim: The boundary formation index attests to the efficacy of the MOSES-enabled measures across independent datasets.
source: and the boundary formation index attests to the efficacy of the MOSES-enabled measures across independent datasets.
evidence: This is stated as validation of MOSES measures.

claim: MOSES' meshes and tracks present a systematic framework for users to define extensive sets of custom measures to comprehensively characterise complex motion phenotypes.
source: Finally, and uniquely, MOSES' meshes and tracks present a systematic framework for users to define extensive sets of custom measures to comprehensively characterise complex motion phenotypes, such as the investigated boundary formation behaviour between epithelial cells.
evidence: This is stated as a unique capability of MOSES.

claim: MOSES successfully constructed feature descriptors to generate interpretable motion maps for the large video dataset.
source: By exploiting this, we successfully constructed feature descriptors to generate interpretable motion maps for our large video dataset.
evidence: This is stated as an achievement using MOSES.

claim: MOSES combines the advantages of existing PIV and single-cell tracking methods to provide a single systematic approach for the analysis of complex motion and interaction patterns.
source: We have shown that MOSES combines the advantages of existing PIV and single-cell tracking methods to provide a single systematic approach for the analysis of complex motion and interaction patterns.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of MOSES' capabilities.

claim: MOSES' operating principle builds upon two established and highly successful approaches, long-time trajectories and graphs/meshes.
source: Its operating principle builds upon two established and highly successful approaches, long-time trajectories and graphs/meshes.
evidence: This describes the foundation of MOSES.

claim: In computer vision, spatio-temporal 'signatures' constructed using long-time trajectories have proven superior to 'signatures' derived from PIV-type motion fields for encoding complex spatio-temporal events such as human actions in very large datasets.
source: In computer vision, spatio-temporal 'signatures' constructed using long-time trajectories have proven superior to 'signatures' derived from PIV-type motion fields for encoding complex spatio-temporal events such as human actions in very large datasets (Wang et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation.

claim: Meshes/graphs are ubiquitously regarded as one of the best approaches to capture relationships between 'objects' across many disciplines.
source: Meshes/graphs are ubiquitously regarded as one of the best approaches to capture relationships between 'objects' across many disciplines, from Google search to protein-protein interaction networks (Szklarczyk et al., 2015), flocking analyses (Ballerini et al., 2008; Zhou et al., 2013; Shishika et al., 2014), to detection of cell jamming in biological physics (Lačević et al., 2003; Park et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: MOSES uniquely brings together the disparate uses of long-time trajectories and meshes into one general analysis framework.
source: MOSES uniquely brings together these disparate uses of long-time trajectories and meshes into one general analysis framework.
evidence: This is stated as a unique contribution of MOSES.

claim: MOSES satisfies the four criteria (robust, sensitive, automatic, and unbiased) necessary for characterising and establishing new phenotypes from live cell imaging.
source: As a result, MOSES satisfies the four criteria (robust, sensitive, automatic, and unbiased) necessary for characterising and establishing new phenotypes from live cell imaging.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about MOSES' capabilities.

claim: The analysis of datasets that include variable quality videos and experiments with a small number of replicates demonstrates the potential of the proposed computational framework.
source: The analysis of datasets that include variable quality videos and experiments with a small number of replicates demonstrates the potential of the proposed computational framework.
evidence: This is stated as evidence of MOSES' robustness.

claim: MOSES is progress towards overcoming the individual limitations of single-cell tracking and PIV-type velocity methods.
source: Importantly, MOSES is progress towards overcoming the individual limitations of single-cell tracking and PIV-type velocity methods.
evidence: This is stated as a key contribution of MOSES.

claim: Single-cell tracks are notoriously problematic over long times; the track of a single cell may be lost or broken into many separate tracks.
source: Single-cell tracks are notoriously problematic over long times; the track of a single cell may be lost or broken into many separate tracks.
evidence: This is stated as a known limitation of single-cell tracking.

claim: MOSES superpixel tracks avoids the problems of single-cell tracks and recovers the global motion patterns.
source: MOSES superpixel tracks avoids this and recovers the global motion patterns (c.f. motion saliency maps, derived measures and motion signatures).
evidence: This is stated as an advantage of MOSES.

claim: Side-by-side comparison of MOSES and the standard PIV method using published datasets demonstrates that MOSES not only enables all the measurements of PIV, but by further exploiting long-time tracks and neighbourhood relationships, delivers greater physical and biological insights.
source: Side-by-side comparison of MOSES and the standard PIV method using published datasets demonstrates that MOSES not only enables all the measurements of PIV, but by further exploiting long-time tracks and neighbourhood relationships, delivers greater physical and biological insights.
evidence: This is stated as a result from the comparison.

claim: Complex salient spatio-temporal motion patterns and events such as boundary formation, deformation waves due to cell jamming between two cell populations and cell death can all be quantitatively captured by MOSES.
source: Complex salient spatio-temporal motion patterns and events such as boundary formation, deformation waves due to cell jamming between two cell populations and cell death can all be quantitatively captured by MOSES.
evidence: This is stated as a capability of MOSES.

claim: The ability of MOSES to perform long-time tracking (up to 6 days demonstrated in this study) enabled spatial localisation of the cell populations involved in a particular motion phenotype.
source: Critically, the ability of MOSES to perform long-time tracking (up to 6 days demonstrated in this study) enabled spatial localisation of the cell populations involved in a particular motion phenotype.
evidence: This is stated as a key capability of MOSES, with quantitative evidence.

claim: MOSES does not require complex user settings to facilitate reproducibility in analyses.
source: MOSES does not require complex user settings to facilitate reproducibility in analyses because it does not aim to threshold or cluster out the moving objects or phenotypes during analysis, which would introduce intermediate processing errors.
evidence: This is stated as a design feature of MOSES.

claim: MOSES' philosophy is to facilitate systematic generation of many motion-related measurements based on trajectory and mesh statistics sufficient for applying machine learning methods for data-driven object segmentation, video classification and phenotype detection in large video collections with minimum prior information.
source: Rather its philosophy is to facilitate systematic generation of many motion-related measurements based on trajectory and mesh statistics sufficient for applying machine learning methods for data-driven object segmentation, video classification and phenotype detection in large video collections (e.g. Figure 5, motion map) with minimum prior information.
evidence: This describes the design philosophy of MOSES.

claim: The main parameter the user specifies in MOSES is the number of initial superpixels, which determines the spatial resolution of analysis.
source: The main parameter the user specifies is the number of initial superpixels, which determines the spatial resolution of analysis.
evidence: This describes the main user input for MOSES.

claim: No complicated fitting of complex models and no special hardware such as GPUs are required for MOSES.
source: No complicated fitting of complex models and no special hardware such as GPUs are required.
evidence: This is stated as a practical advantage of MOSES.

claim: MOSES is modular and its components can be readily adapted to suit specific applications.
source: MOSES is modular and its components can be readily adapted to suit specific applications, for example non-square superpixel shapes to better capture cells that undergo large shape changes.
evidence: This is stated as a design feature of MOSES.

claim: Analysis of 96 videos with 1344 × 1024 pixel resolution and 145 frames by tracking 1000 superpixels takes under 4 h on an unoptimized code implementation running on a single PC (3.2 GHz, 16 GB RAM).
source: Analysis of 96 videos with 1344 × 1024 pixel resolution and 145 frames by tracking 1000 superpixels takes under 4 h on an unoptimized code implementation running on a single PC (3.2 GHz, 16 GB RAM).
evidence: This is a quantitative statement about MOSES' computational efficiency.

claim: MOSES results are stored efficiently (~1–2 MB per video) compared to ~0.1–1 GB per video for full spatio-temporal PIV/optical flow motion fields.
source: Results are stored efficiently (~1–2 MB per video) compared to ~0.1–1 GB per video, depending on the subsampling used to save the full spatio-temporal PIV/optical flow motion fields.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of storage efficiency.

claim: MOSES is particularly useful for unbiased explorative high-content screening with an aim to discover fundamental principles of cellular motion dynamics in biology and to identify factors or drugs that alter cellular motion dynamics in disease aetiology and treatment.
source: It is particularly useful for unbiased explorative high-content screening with an aim to discover fundamental principles of cellular motion dynamics in biology and to identify factors or drugs that alter cellular motion dynamics in disease aetiology and treatment.
evidence: This is stated as a key application of MOSES.
